morning.text: Morning! You'll be the new clerk. Gus Penrose, porter. I bring in the strays off the platforms.
Mrs Pell left you her desk just as she kept it. Forty-one years she sat there. Said you'd know what to do.
Last night's lot is in the drawers and on the shelf, tagged. Ring the bell when you're ready for the first one!

Welcome, love. You'll do fine. It runs in the family.

I've left you one rule a day. That's plenty to be going on with.

intro.text: Morning. I've lost my wallet, haven't I. Clean out of my apron pocket.
{Brown leather|leather}. I had it on the {Harwick stopper|train} first thing this morning.
There's a photo of my dog in it. {Biscuit|photo}. Best sausage dog in Harwick.

claims.text: Lost on the Harwick stopper, this morning
A photo of his dog Biscuit inside

answers.text: That's Biscuit! Lovely ears, terrible manners.
W.B. Walter Bix. Mother had them pressed in for my fortieth.
Harwick, same as every morning. The ovens don't light themselves.

notMine.text: That's not mine, love. Mine's brown leather, with a photo of a dog in it.

verdicts.ledger: Walter's story matched the tag, the photo of Biscuit and the initials.

reply.text: That's the one! Hello, Biscuit, you daft sausage.
Pop in to the bakery on Canal Row. There's a bun in it for you.

verdicts.ledger: Walter's story matched the tag, the photograph and the initials. It was his.

reply.text: But... that's my Biscuit in there. Right. I'll manage.

verdicts.ledger: There's nothing strange about a baker's wallet. It should have gone home.

reply.text: You're locking my wallet in a safe? That's daft, that is!

intro.text: Sorry, sorry to bother you. I've lost my scarf. It's {red, and knitted|scarf}.
I left it in the {waiting room|where}, I think? This morning, before the 8.40.
My Nan knitted it. There's a little {hole near one end|hole}. I keep meaning to darn it.

claims.text: Left in the waiting room this morning
Has a hole near one end

answers.text: The moths got it! Nan would be furious.
Nan sews a label into everything. "Knitted with love." She means it, too.

notMine.text: Oh, no, sorry, that's not mine. Mine's a red scarf.

verdicts.ledger: Clementine knew about the moth hole, and Nan's label was underneath.

reply.text: Oh, thank you! Nan would never have forgiven me.

verdicts.ledger: Clementine knew about the hole and the label underneath. It was hers.
It was an ordinary scarf. It should have gone home.

reply.text: Is that a safe? For a scarf?

cases.hint: Something feels off? Click a finding on the claim slip to ask about it.

intro.text: Afternoon, squire. Reggie Stokes. I'll be quick, I'm a busy man.
My brolly. {Green, with a duck's head for a handle|umbrella}. Left it on {Platform 5|where}, Sunday evening.
Lovely piece. Sentimental value. You'll have seen it. It's right there on your shelf.

claims.text: A green umbrella with a duck's-head handle

answers.text: A name? No, no. Plain as anything. I don't hold with writing on things.
Not a mark on it. I look after my things.

notMine.text: That's not it, squire. Green. Duck. Come on.

verdicts.ledger: Reggie read the tag off the shelf. He didn't know the name under the strap: B. BRAMBLE.

reply.text: Worth a try, wasn't it? No harm done, squire.

verdicts.ledger: Reggie said it was plain and unmarked. A name was hidden under the strap, B. BRAMBLE, and the beak was chipped.
Nothing uncanny about it. It just wasn't his. Refuse him, and the real owner will come.

reply.text: Here, what's that for? It's a brolly!

intro.text: Hello, dear. I've come about my case.
A {brown case|case}. Leather. I put it down for just a moment, and...
When? Oh, goodness. It might have been a {Tuesday|when}. It might have been 1934.
Is that humming? How lovely. It always did that when I came home.

claims.text: Lost on a Tuesday. Or in 1934

answers.text: Odile Marsh. O.M. My husband had them put on the year we married.
Lisbon! I was twenty-one and ate nothing but custard tarts. And Vienna. I danced every dance.
Lavender, from my mother's garden. It never fades, does it?

notMine.text: No, dear, that isn't mine. Can't you hear which one is singing?

verdicts.ledger: The case hummed for Mrs Marsh. Things that hum know their owners.

reply.text: There you are. There you are.
Oh, I feel twenty-one again. Thank you, dear.

verdicts.ledger: It hummed the moment she arrived. Things that hum know their owners.

reply.text: Oh. Well. I'll come back another time, dear. I always do.

verdicts.ledger: Humming isn't danger. It's recognition. It should have gone home with her.

reply.text: You're locking it away? But it's mine. Can't you hear it?

evening.text: That's the lot! Not bad for a first day.
Oh, one more thing. This came in on the last train off Platform 9. It's... well. Have a look for yourself.

gazette.headline: WOMAN, 94, REUNITED WITH LUGGAGE LOST IN 1934
gazette.body: Mrs Odile Marsh of Canal Row collected a suitcase from Ninefold Lost Property yesterday, twenty-eight years after leaving it on a Vienna platform. "It hummed," she told our reporter. "It always did."

gazette.headline: NEW CLERK FOR NINEFOLD LOST PROPERTY
gazette.body: Mrs Agnes Pell, who ran the Lost Property Office for forty-one years, has retired. Her replacement began work yesterday. Commuters are reminded that unclaimed property is kept for one week, or longer, at the clerk's discretion.
